traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
title: Thrombocytopenia & Coagulation Emergencies: ITP, TTP, DIC & HIT
html:
Thrombocytopenia is a finding, not a diagnosis. One patient may have immune platelet destruction and primarily bleeding risk; another may have platelet consumption in dangerous microvascular thrombosis; a third may be bleeding and clotting simultaneously. The RN must validate the trend, assess the patient before the number, identify the pattern and trigger, protect the patient from preventable bleeding, and escalate time-critical syndromes without waiting for every confirmatory result.

Learning goals

  • Assess bleeding severity and distinguish platelet-pattern bleeding from coagulation-factor-pattern bleeding.
  • Differentiate immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT).
  • Recognize neurologic, cardiac, renal, limb, pulmonary, and hemodynamic emergencies despite a low platelet count.
  • Implement disorder-specific precautions and prepare prescribed immune therapy, plasma exchange, blood components, or non-heparin anticoagulation safely.
  • Evaluate response with symptoms, organ function, bleeding and thrombosis findings, and serial laboratory trends.

Assess the patient before reacting to the count

Confirm the platelet trend, previous baseline, specimen quality, medications and heparin exposure, recent infection, pregnancy, cancer, autoimmune disease, liver or splenic disease, transfusion, surgery, trauma, and current treatment. Unexpected isolated thrombocytopenia may reflect platelet clumping in the collection tube; follow the laboratory's verification or recollection process. Do not let verification delay emergency care when the patient has active bleeding, neurologic change, shock, or suspected thrombosis.

Inspect skin and oral mucosa for petechiae, purpura, bruising, gum bleeding, and blood-filled blisters. Ask about epistaxis, heavy menstrual bleeding, hematuria, melena, hematemesis, headache, vision or speech change, weakness, chest pain, dyspnea, abdominal or back pain, limb swelling, and urine output. Platelet disorders often cause mucocutaneous bleeding, while coagulation-factor deficiencies more often cause deep-tissue bleeding or hemarthrosis, but mixed disorders and severe bleeding can break this pattern.

Bleeding severity outranks one platelet threshold

A falling platelet count increases concern, but the number alone does not determine treatment. Intracranial, airway, gastrointestinal, retroperitoneal, obstetric, or hemodynamically significant bleeding is an emergency at any count. Assess airway, breathing, circulation, neurologic status, perfusion, pain, visible and occult losses, medication exposure, and access sites. Notify the appropriate response team, establish ordered access and testing, protect the airway, and prepare blood products or reversal treatment according to the suspected cause and authorized plan.

Until the plan is clarified, reduce avoidable trauma: use gentle oral and skin care, fall prevention, prolonged pressure after venipuncture, and the smallest necessary needle; avoid intramuscular injections, rectal procedures, unnecessary urinary catheterization, and unapproved aspirin or NSAIDs. Do not automatically restrict all activity or transfuse platelets for every low count. Mobility, procedures, prophylaxis, and transfusion must reflect bleeding, diagnosis, count trend, comorbidities, and local policy.

ITP: immune platelet destruction with variable bleeding

ITP is an immune-mediated platelet disorder and often presents as isolated thrombocytopenia with petechiae, purpura, mucosal bleeding, or no symptoms. It is a diagnosis of exclusion: review the smear, other blood-cell lines, medications, infection and autoimmune context, liver and spleen findings, and alternative causes. A normal coagulation panel does not prove ITP, and an isolated low platelet count does not exclude a dangerous mimic.

Treatment depends on bleeding severity, platelet count and trend, age, comorbidities, anticoagulant or antiplatelet use, lifestyle, and patient preferences. Observation may be appropriate for selected patients, while corticosteroids, immune globulin, thrombopoietin-receptor agonists, rituximab, fostamatinib, splenectomy, or other strategies may be chosen by hematology. In critical bleeding, prepare combined emergency measures and platelet support as ordered; a platelet transfusion alone may have only a temporary effect because immune destruction continues. Monitor for therapy-specific infection, glucose, blood pressure, thrombosis, hepatic, and infusion risks.

TTP: thrombocytopenia plus microangiopathic hemolysis is an emergency

TTP is a thrombotic microangiopathy associated with severe ADAMTS13 deficiency. Platelet-rich microthrombi injure organs and mechanically fragment red cells. Think of TTP when thrombocytopenia occurs with microangiopathic hemolytic anemia: schistocytes, rising lactate dehydrogenase and indirect bilirubin, low haptoglobin, anemia, and a usually negative direct antiglobulin test in the proper context. Neurologic change, headache, seizure, stroke-like findings, chest pain, myocardial injury, fever, or kidney dysfunction may occur.

Do not wait for the classic five-part pentad; many patients do not present with every feature. Obtain the ordered ADAMTS13 sample before plasma treatment when feasible, but suspected acquired TTP is time-critical and specialist-directed treatment should not be delayed while the result is pending. Activate hematology urgently and prepare therapeutic plasma exchange, corticosteroid or other immunosuppression, and caplacizumab according to the current plan. Monitor neurologic status, rhythm, troponin when ordered, urine output, renal function, hemolysis, platelets, access complications, infection, and treatment-related bleeding. Platelet transfusion is not a routine response to the count in TTP and requires specialist direction, particularly because the disease is thrombotic.

DIC: uncontrolled coagulation consumes platelets and factors

DIC is secondary to another major illness such as sepsis, severe trauma, obstetric catastrophe, malignancy, or extensive tissue injury. Systemic coagulation activation produces microvascular thrombosis and organ ischemia while consuming platelets and coagulation factors, so bleeding and clotting can coexist. Look for oozing from lines or wounds, ecchymoses, mucosal or gastrointestinal bleeding, cool or mottled skin, digital ischemia, respiratory or neurologic deterioration, oliguria, hypotension, and progression of the underlying trigger.

Interpret serial trends rather than a single panel. A falling platelet count, prolonged clotting times, falling fibrinogen, elevated fibrin breakdown markers, schistocytes, and worsening organ function can support the pattern, but liver disease, massive bleeding, transfusion, and other conditions may overlap. Immediate priority is treatment of the cause and restoration of perfusion. Prepare prescribed plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen replacement, red cells, anticoagulation in selected thrombotic presentations, and source-control therapy according to bleeding, laboratory results, and specialist direction. Reassess temperature, perfusion, access sites, urine output, mental status, oxygenation, laboratory trends, and response to the causal treatment.

HIT: the danger is thrombosis, not simply bleeding

HIT is an immune prothrombotic reaction to heparin. Suspect it from the magnitude and timing of the platelet fall, new thrombosis or skin reaction, and absence of a stronger alternative cause—not from any low platelet count in a person receiving heparin. A fall of more than half from baseline can matter even if the final value remains above the usual thrombocytopenia threshold. Use the validated 4Ts pretest score with complete, accurate data rather than intuition alone, and recalculate if the clinical picture changes.

When the clinical pathway identifies suspected HIT, stop all heparin sources as ordered—including infusions, prophylaxis, flushes, and heparin-coated exposure—and prepare the prescribed non-heparin anticoagulant and confirmatory testing. Assess for deep-vein thrombosis, pulmonary embolism, limb ischemia, stroke, myocardial infarction, adrenal injury, and catheter thrombosis. Do not substitute warfarin or give platelets independently during acute HIT; these decisions require the HIT protocol and specialist plan. Document the reaction and communicate it across settings.

Compare the four patterns

ITP: primarily immune platelet destruction; often isolated thrombocytopenia and mucocutaneous bleeding. TTP: thrombocytopenia plus red-cell fragmentation and organ ischemia; normal or near-normal routine coagulation times may occur because this is a platelet-rich microangiopathy. DIC: systemic consumption of platelets and coagulation factors from a major trigger; both bleeding and thrombosis, with evolving coagulation abnormalities. HIT: heparin-associated immune thrombosis; focus on timing, proportional platelet fall, and new clot rather than bleeding alone.

The same platelet count can therefore require different actions. Giving platelets reflexively, withholding all thrombosis prevention, or assuming petechiae establishes ITP can cause harm. State the full pattern during escalation: count and rate of fall, bleeding, thrombotic or neurologic findings, hemolysis evidence, coagulation trend, trigger, heparin timing, organ function, and current therapies.

Apply clinical judgment

  1. Recognize cues: Identify bleeding location and severity, platelet baseline and trend, other cell lines, smear and hemolysis findings, coagulation pattern, heparin timing, trigger, and organ changes.
  2. Analyze cues: Decide whether the pattern suggests isolated immune destruction, thrombotic microangiopathy, systemic consumption, heparin-associated thrombosis, artifact, or another cause.
  3. Prioritize hypotheses: Intracranial or airway bleeding, shock, suspected TTP, DIC with organ failure, and HIT with new thrombosis outrank routine precautions.
  4. Generate solutions: Activate hematology and emergency pathways, treat the underlying trigger, prepare disorder-specific therapy, reduce avoidable trauma, and coordinate laboratory and blood-bank support.
  5. Take action: Escalate exact trends, give authorized treatment, stop heparin when the HIT pathway directs it, monitor plasma exchange and infusions, and never transfuse from the count alone.
  6. Evaluate outcomes: Confirm controlled bleeding, stable neurologic and cardiopulmonary function, restored perfusion and urine output, improving platelet and hemolysis trends, treatment of the cause, and absence of new thrombosis or therapy toxicity.

Clinical example

A patient arrives with confusion, petechiae, platelets of 18,000/µL, falling hemoglobin, schistocytes, rising LDH, and normal routine coagulation times. The RN does not label the case as uncomplicated ITP or wait for the ADAMTS13 result. The RN performs frequent neurologic and cardiopulmonary assessment, activates urgent hematology evaluation, obtains time-sensitive ordered specimens, prepares central-access and plasma-exchange support, avoids an independent platelet transfusion, and monitors for cardiac, renal, bleeding, and treatment complications.
